reasons: Simple and deterministic, which makes it easy to reason about.
No test in the packet checks the tier outcomes.
The relationship rule is intentionally unexplained, which can leave a user unsure why a signal is not Tier 1.

sections.name: EvidenceTier
sections.title: The four evidence grades
sections.what: Defines the four evidence grades used for signals, C1 to C4, from strongest to weakest lead. These grades decide which tier a signal can reach.
sections.why: The code comment says tiers are a rule set over the research mapping, so the grade is the key input.
sections.watch_out: Grades are fixed text, so any new grade must be added here and in the rules together.

sections.name: TierRules
sections.title: The shape of the tier settings
sections.what: Lists the settings that decide tiers: how recent a source must be, what Tier 1 requires, what Tier 2 requires, which grades count as weak leads, and whether codebook focus caps or lifts a signal.
sections.why: The code comment says the defaults can be tuned by teams in the codebook.
sections.watch_out: Changing these values changes the tiers of all signals at once on the next read.

sections.name: DEFAULT_TIER_RULES
sections.title: Default tier settings
sections.what: Sets the defaults: sources within 180 days, Tier 1 needs C1 or C2 evidence with value at risk, a decision window, severity of at least 4, ability to act of at least 3 and a relationship. Tier 2 needs C1 or C2 evidence and a score of at least 55. C4 is a weak lead. Focus capping and lifting are both on.
sections.why: The code comment says the defaults reproduce the original rules.
sections.watch_out: A codebook can override these defaults, so the defaults are not always what users see.

sections.name: TierInputs
sections.title: What a tier calculation needs
sections.what: Lists the inputs: evidence grade, value at risk, decision window, severity, ability to act, total score, access level, publication dates and codebook focus.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the names of the inputs.
sections.watch_out: Focus is optional and defaults to zero, so forgetting to pass it silently removes codebook effects.

sections.name: computeTier
sections.title: Decides the priority tier of a signal
sections.what: Gives Tier 1 when every strict rule is met, including the relationship rule. Otherwise gives Tier 2 when the signal is recent, has C1 or C2 evidence and reaches the score threshold, and Tier 3 for the rest. Weak leads are Tier 4 at once. Codebook focus then caps deprioritised signals at Tier 3 and lifts prioritised Tier 3 signals to Tier 2 when they qualify. Returns the tier with plain reasons.
sections.why: The code comment says the relationship rule is hidden because access is a server-only value.
sections.watch_out: The relationship rule can cause a Tier 1 miss that the listed reasons do not mention, so a reader may see a reason that is not the real cause.

summary: Decides each signal's priority tier, from 1 (most actionable) to 4 (weak lead), using fixed rules the team can adjust.
purpose: Sorts signals so the strongest, most actionable ones are seen first.
why: The header comment says the rules are deterministic, the defaults reproduce the original rules, and tiers are recomputed on every read so a rule change applies at once.
how: 1. A weakest-grade evidence result returns Tier 4 immediately. 2. Checks the Tier 1 rules and lists any that are missing. 3. Applies a relationship rule that is not explained to users. 4. Falls to Tier 2 when the signal is recent, has strong enough evidence, and reaches the score threshold. 5. Otherwise Tier 3. 6. Adjusts for codebook focus: a deprioritised signal is capped at Tier 3, and a prioritised Tier 3 is lifted to Tier 2 when it qualifies. 7. Returns the tier and plain reasons.
inputs: A signal's evidence grade, value at risk, decision window, severity, ability to act, total score, access level, publication dates, codebook focus, and optionally a set of rules.
outputs: A tier number and a list of plain-English reasons explaining it.
risks: The relationship rule is applied without its reason being shown, so a user may not understand why a signal is not Tier 1. Publication dates in the future are ignored. A missing focus value means no codebook effect. The Tier 1 check only tests whether value at risk is present, not whether it is good.
debug: Read the reasons list first, since it explains each decision. If a signal is unexpectedly Tier 3, check its publication dates (recent means within 180 days by default) and its evidence grade. If a Tier 1 result is missing, the relationship rule is a likely cause. If a cap or lift seems wrong, check the codebook focus.
